        GOOD COMPANYASSOOCIATES COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION'S
                     PROPOSAL FOR ADOPTION (PFA)


We appreciate the Commission's prompt action in advancingthe proposed rule under
Project 58481, which is important to addressingthe unprecedented demand for
interconnection to the ERCOT grid. We recognize the substantial effort that has gone into
developingthe final language and addressing a wide range of complex issues. In that spirit,
we respectfully offer the following comments and suggestions regarding certain provisions
where additionalclarification or refinement may be helpfulto support consistent
implementation and avoid unintended consequences.

Given the limited time available, we briefly highlight several sections that may benefit from
furtherconsideration.

1. Clarify Applicability Thresholds for Existing Large Loads
(b) Applicability.
The language in (b)(1) indicates that the rule applies to loads that have not energized but
are or will reach the 75 MW for the first time with their requested interconnection. It also
states that the rule applies to loads over 75 MW that are requestingto expand by 75 MW or
more.
Our concern lies with the language in (b)(2) which states that "For a large load customer
that seeks an expanded interconnection, this section applies to the incremental load
addition." On its face, this language reads that the rule will apply to an existing large load
customer of 75 MW or larger that requests to expand even by one incremental MW. This
reading is inconsistent with the preamble discussion on pages 47- 48 which states that
"the adopted rule strikes an appropriate balance of ensuringthatinterconnection requests
significantly impactingtransmission needs are required to comply with the adopted rule
while not requiring compliance for incremental requests that do not significantly impact
transmission needs in that the adopted rule does not require compliance for loads that
expand by less than 75 MW unless the load is surpassing 75 MW forthe first time.
 To resolve this inconsistency, we suggest adding clarifying language as follows:
        (2) For a large load customerthat seeks an expanded interconnection of 75 MW or
        more. this section appliestothe incremental requested load addition.

2. Align the Definition of "End-Use Customer" with ERCOT FAQ definition
(c) Definitions, (8) End-use customer.
While this would seem a simple matter, this definition ("The entitythat ultimately
consumes power") is a change to the definition that is used by ERCOT in determining
eligibility forthe Batch Zero process. This may create an issue when the party responsible
for electricity consumption is a tenant occupyingthe site under a lease agreement, rather
than the owner of the property. We suggest, to be clear and align with previous discussion,
that it be worded as follows:
        (8) End-use customer- The entitythat ultimately consumes power orthe entitythat
        has executed a retail electric service agreement.

3. Clarify Open-Ended Water Information Requirements
(d) Intermediate agreement. (1) Required disclosures. (F) Water. (v) "any other related
information."
This was no doubt appended to allow the utilityto obtain any information of importance,
particularly given the widespread concern about the impact of data centers on local water
use. Becausetimeis short, we understand whya somewhatopen-ended requirement
would make sense here. However, in the rule as stated, it puts the large load customer in
jeopardy for not filing "any other related information" without limitation. That is, it puts the
obligation on the large load customerto anticipate what is needed and leaves it vulnerable
to later determination that something"related" was not filed. We suggestthe language
simple be expanded to read as follows:
       (v) any other related information requested by the utility.

This would allow the utility to request and obtain any related information sought, without
leaving a vague requirement that customers will have a hard time knowing how to comply
with, and investors will perceive as another compliance risk.

4.   Limit Material Modification Requirements to ERCOT-Defined Changes
(e) Interconnection study. (4) New interconnection request required.
The language in this section, which requires a large load undergoing a material change to
go through the next batch process, is too broad or too vague. The explicit addition of "or
any other modification" in particular is so encompassing as to present a significant risk for
 investors. Any industrial facility goes through changes over time that may include routine
exchange of onsite equipment. We recommend changes as follows:
        (4) New interconnection request required. A large load customerthat materially
        changes its interconnection request, as described in ERCOT protocols orguides,
        includingbychangingits requested pcakdcmand, phased cncrgization schedule,
        point of interconnection, site configuration, load composition, load type, or any
        other modification, must submit a new interconnection request to the
        interconnecting DSP orthe interconnecting TSR


5.   Narrow Financial Security Forfeiture Provisions
(f) SLLIA (3) Return and forfeiture of financial security (D) Forfeiture.
This section proposes a severe penalty for what could be read as ANY failure to comply
with an SLLIA for any amount of time. This seems to be in conflict with the section (g) that
allows for up to 24 months of delays, which we assume was adopted in recognition that
some changes, or delays are unforeseeable and unavoidable, and no fault of any party. We
appreciate that the commission gives the utility some flexibility by usingthe word "may" to
give permission but not "must," to require forfeiture of all financial security. If, however, the
intent was to have this a failure to meet its minimum billing commitment or other financial
commitments, then it should be narrowed to address that issue. As written, it represents a
significant risk for investors.

6. Clarify Treatment of Non-Utilized Transmission Capacity
(g) Non-utilized transmission capacity. (2)(E).
This section states:
        (2) Within 60 days of providing notice to ERCOT under this subsection, the
        interconnectingTSP mustdraw down onthe large load customer's financialsecurity
        and apply the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed. Outstanding
        amounts owed include the following:
               (E) the large load minimum billingdemand described in Section §25.193 of
               this title forthe set period of time described in Section §25.193.
The above excerpt of the rule would appear to require a drawdown of the security for the
entire project's demand or interconnection capacity allocation, rather than for that portion
which is to be reallocated due to failure to fully use the allocation within 24 months of the
original schedule. As written, this reads as if the failure to reach full capacity of an
interconnection allocation would lead to the required collection of all future minimum
billing amounts on demand, forthe entire capacity, conceivably for the forecast life of the
project or longer.
 Most importantly we requestthe commission modifythe language first to specifythis draw
on the financial security only applies to the amount of allocation to be reallocated due to
disuse. Secondly, we suggest that the payments for such costs be due over time as they
would normally have been billed had the customer's consumption reached its final
projected demand. Thirdly we suggest that payment be limited to the minimum billing
requirement of the unused capacity until such time as the capacity is reallocated for use by
anotherend-use customer, to again avoid double billing, oraddingunnecessaryadditional
financial riskto the process for prospective investors.


7.   Provide Utility Discretion Regarding Financial Security Drawdowns
(h) Batch zero load. (1) Financial security posted under ERCOT Planning Guide Section
9, as of the effective date of this section. (ii).
This paragraph requires the utility "must" draw down the financial security if a payment on
an invoice is made after a 1 0th business day. The utility should have the option to help
supportenforcement, butthis action can be complexand burdensome if the utility knows a
payment will be made, and there is no history of non-payment of malfeasance. We
recommend a simple change to "may"to allow the utility to use its judgment.
        (ii) The interconnecting DSP orthe interconnecting TSP may elect to either invoice
        the large load customer for outstanding amounts owed; or draw down on the large
        load customer's financialsecurityand applythe financialsecurity to outstanding
        amounts owed. If the large load customer fails to pay an invoice from the
        interconnecting DSP orthe interconnecting TSP within 10 working days after the
        receipt of an invoice, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must may
        draw down on the large load customer's financial security for the amounts invoiced.




Good Company Associates appreciates consideration of these important comments as the
Commission considersthe Proposal forAdoption.
